title: Qawwali
description: Qawwali is Sufi devotional ensemble singing at the dargahs of the Deccan — patronised alongside Hindustani classical music by the Asaf Jahi court, and still sung on Thursday evenings at the shrines of Gulbarga and Hyderabad.
dedication: In memory of the Asaf Jahi dynasty
subtitle: Sufi Devotional Singing · The Deccan Dargahs

items.value: Sufi devotional ensemble singing at shrines
Asaf Jahi Hyderabad, alongside Hindustani classical music
The dargahs of Gulbarga and Yousufain Sharif, Hyderabad
Opens with verses by Amir Khusrau, closes with verses by Wali Deccani

blocks.intro: Qawwali is Sufi devotional ensemble singing performed at the dargahs of the Deccan. The Asaf Jahi court patronised it alongside Hindustani classical music, and singers travelled freely between durbar and dargah — but its deepest home has always been the shrine itself.

body: The Asaf Jahi court patronised both Hindustani classical music and the qawwali sung at Sufi shrines, and singers moved freely between the two worlds — the same artists who performed at durbar also sang at dargah.<cite data-ref="leonard-1978"></cite>

sections.sub: An unbroken line of poetry, sung every week
body: On any Thursday at the dargah of Khwaja Bandanawaz in Gulbarga, or at Yousufain Sharif in Hyderabad, qawwals open the evening with verses by Amir Khusrau and close with verses by Wali Deccani — a line of poetry running unbroken from the fourteenth century.<cite data-ref="ernst-lawrence-2002"></cite>

references.text: Karen Leonard, Social History of an Indian Caste: The Kayasths of Hyderabad, University of California Press, 1978.
Carl W. Ernst & Bruce B. Lawrence, Sufi Martyrs of Love: The Chishti Order in South Asia and Beyond, Palgrave Macmillan, 2002.
